analogy.p: Presenting and analysing data is like telling a story using a photo album. You choose the clearest photographs (graphs and maps), caption each one (titles, labels), point out the main plot (the trend), the surprise (an anomaly) and the reason it happened (geographical explanation). It breaks down because a story can be invented, whereas in geography every statement must be backed by evidence from the data.

bullets: You must **select and justify** suitable presentation techniques for your own data.
You must be able to **draw, complete and interpret** graphs and maps, including those in unfamiliar fieldwork.
You must be able to **calculate and use** the mean, median, mode, range and interquartile range, and percentages.
You must **describe** trends, relationships and anomalies using figures from the data.
You must **explain** patterns using geographical theory (for example the Bradshaw model or distance decay).
Presentation and analysis come before the **conclusion and evaluation** (the next stage of the enquiry).
Command words include **describe, suggest, calculate, explain, assess** and **justify**.
core.h: What the specification requires you to know
core.p: After collecting data, the AQA specification expects you to **present** it in suitable ways and then **analyse** it. Presentation means choosing **graphs, maps, tables and diagrams** that suit the type of data. Analysis means describing **patterns, trends, anomalies and relationships**, using **statistical measures** where suitable, and explaining the results using geographical ideas. Paper 3 Section B tests this on both your own fieldwork and on unfamiliar data printed in the paper.

bullets: **Bar chart**: bars separated by gaps, for **discrete or categorised data** such as land-use type or number of people at each site.
**Pie chart**: shows **proportions of a whole**, e.g. percentage of shops by type; best with few categories.
**Histogram**: bars touch, for **continuous grouped data** such as pebble size in classes of 10 mm.
**Line graph**: shows **change over time or distance**, with points joined; the line shows a trend.
**Scattergraph**: plots **two variables** to see if there is a **relationship** (correlation).

**Kite diagram, radial graph and dispersion graph** are other options: kite diagrams show change along a transect; radial graphs show direction or categories round a circle; dispersion graphs show **spread** of data.
**Maps**: choropleth, isoline, proportional symbols, dot and flow-line maps show **spatial patterns**.
**Annotated photographs and field sketches** present **qualitative** information such as building condition or river features.
core.h: Choosing the right type of presentation
core.p: The best method depends on the **type of data** and on the **question**. Figure 1 gives a quick guide. A good choice makes the pattern easy to see, so a graph that hides the trend, such as a pie chart used for 20 sites, is a poor choice. Examiners reward answers that **name the technique**, say what it shows, and give a reason it suits the data.

bullets: Choose a scale that uses **at least half of the grid** and starts at zero unless there is a reason not to.
Equal intervals on each axis: **do not skip or squash numbers**.
On a **line graph or scattergraph**, plot points with a small neat cross or dot and draw a **ruler line** or a line of best fit.
A **line of best fit** is a straight line (or smooth curve) with about the **same number of points above and below**; it does not have to pass through the origin.
On a **histogram**, bars touch and the x-axis shows continuous classes.
On a **bar chart**, bars have equal widths and gaps and labelled categories.
On a **pie chart**, angle = (value divided by total) x 360 degrees.
Always **label** unusual points (anomalies) in the margin or with a circle.
**Check** your graph against the data table once you have finished.
core.p: Marks for drawing graphs are gained for **accuracy and completeness**, so use a ruler and sharp pencil. Every graph needs a **title**, **labelled axes with units**, an even **scale**, and a **key** if more than one data set is shown. The **independent variable** (such as distance downstream) goes on the **x-axis** and the **dependent variable** (such as velocity) on the **y-axis**. If you complete a graph in an exam, check the scale and plot to the nearest half square.

bullets: **Choropleth map**: areas are shaded by value, with **darker shades for higher values** and a key of classes. It is quick to read but hides variation inside each area.

**Isoline map**: lines join points of **equal value** (e.g. pedestrian flow). **Close lines** show rapid change; wide spacing shows gradual change. Values between sites must be estimated by **interpolation**.
**Proportional symbols**: the **size of the symbol** shows the value, e.g. circles sized by pedestrian count. Easy to compare but large symbols can overlap.
**Dot maps** show **location and density** of items such as shops or sampling points.
**Flow-line maps** use arrows whose **width** shows quantity, e.g. traffic or movement of people.
**GIS** (geographic information systems) can layer data, e.g. putting questionnaire scores over a map of land use.
Add a **title, key, north arrow and scale** to every map you draw.
To describe a map: say **where** values are highest and lowest, mention the **pattern** (e.g. decreasing with distance from the centre), and give **figures** or classes from the key.
core.p: Maps show the **spatial pattern** of your data, such as how environmental quality changes across a town. Fieldwork maps use a **base map** with data added on top, often using colour or symbols. They help to show **clusters**, **gradients** and **zones**. The specification expects you to understand a range of map types, including choropleth maps and isoline maps.

bullets: A good sketch has a **title, location, date and direction**, plus **labels** (names features) and **annotations** (add explanation).
Draw only **important features** and keep outlines simple.
Use a **frame** and show the **foreground, middle ground and background**.
Annotated photos can show **change between sites**, e.g. litter, graffiti or building condition along a transect.
**Interview and questionnaire quotes** can be added to a graph or map to give opinions.
Qualitative data can **support** quantitative data, e.g. photos showing why a depth reading is high.
Weakness: qualitative methods are **subjective**, as different people may notice different things.
core.h: Qualitative presentation: photographs and field sketches
core.p: Not all fieldwork data are numbers. **Annotated photographs** and **field sketches** record what a place looks like and show features that are hard to measure. A field sketch is a simple labelled drawing that highlights key geographical features, not an artistic picture. Annotations should **describe and explain**, so each label gives a feature plus a geographical comment, such as "eroded cliff base: waves cause hydraulic power and abrasion".

bullets: **Mean** = sum of all values divided by the number of values. It uses all of the data but is **affected by anomalies**.
**Median** = the middle value when data are **in order**; with an even number, take the **mean of the two middle values**. It is **not affected by anomalies**.
**Mode** = the most frequent value (or modal class for grouped data).
**Range** = highest value minus lowest value; it shows spread but depends on two extremes only.
**Interquartile range (IQR)** = upper quartile (Q3) minus lower quartile (Q1); it shows the spread of the **middle 50 percent** of the data and ignores extremes.
To find quartiles: put data in order, find the median, then find the median of the lower half (Q1) and the upper half (Q3).
A **small IQR** means values are close together (consistent); a **large IQR** means more variation.
Use the **median** if there are anomalies, and the **mean** if the data are fairly symmetrical.
Show working and give **units**: marks are often awarded for the method.
core.h: Statistical measures: mean, median, mode, range and IQR
core.p: Statistics summarise a data set in a few numbers. The **mean** gives the typical value, the **median** is the middle value, the **mode** is the most common, and the **range** and **interquartile range (IQR)** measure spread. Figure 3 shows them for seven sites. You must be able to calculate them, interpret what they show, and choose the best one for the data set.

bullets: **Percentage** = part divided by whole x 100.
**Percentage change** = (new value minus old value) divided by old value x 100.
A **ratio** compares two amounts, e.g. 3:2; simplify by dividing both numbers by the same factor.
**Rate of change** = change in y divided by change in x, e.g. increase of velocity per kilometre downstream.
**Gradient** = vertical change divided by horizontal distance (use the same units for both).
For **proportional pie charts**, angle = (value divided by total) x 360.
Give an answer to a **sensible level of accuracy**, e.g. 1 decimal place if the data are to 1 decimal place.
Check **units**: write m, m/s, cumecs or % in the answer.
core.p: Fieldwork results are often compared using **percentages** or **ratios**, because they allow fair comparison between different sample sizes. For example, 30 out of 50 people can be compared with 45 out of 100 only when both are written as percentages. Calculation questions are usually worth 1 to 3 marks and are marked for **method as well as the answer**, so write each step.

bullets: Start with the **overall trend**: "Pedestrian counts fall steadily with distance from the CBD".
Add **data** from the graph with units: "from 142 at 0 m to 25 at 600 m".
State **how big** the change is: "a decrease of 117 people per 5 minutes" or "around 82 percent less".
Use **trend words**: increases, decreases, steadily, rapidly, levels off, peaks, fluctuates.
Mention **anomalies**: results that do not fit the pattern.
For a scattergraph, state the **type of correlation**: **positive** (both increase), **negative** (one increases as the other decreases) or **no correlation**.
Describe the **strength**: strong if points are close to the line, weak if scattered.
For maps: describe **patterns of location** (zones, clusters, gradients) with directions.
core.p: A good description says **what** the pattern is, **how much** it changes, and **where or when** it changes, using numbers. A useful structure is **overall trend, evidence, anomaly**. Describe means to say what the data show, not why. Avoid reading every data point; pick the **highest, the lowest and the overall change**.

bullets: **Positive correlation**: as x increases, y increases (e.g. velocity and distance downstream).
**Negative correlation**: as x increases, y decreases (e.g. pedestrian counts and distance from the CBD).
**No correlation**: points scattered with no clear direction.
**Strong** correlation: points close to line; **weak**: points spread.
**Correlation is not causation**: a third factor may explain both variables.
The **line of best fit** helps to predict values, but only within the range of the data (do not extrapolate far beyond it).
A small sample may suggest a correlation by chance, so **more data** make it more reliable.
The **gradient** of the line shows how quickly y changes with x.
core.h: Correlation and what it tells you
core.p: A **correlation** is a relationship between two variables on a scattergraph. It is **strong** when the points lie close to the line of best fit and **weak** when they are scattered. A correlation shows that two things are **linked**, but **correlation does not prove cause**: other factors may be responsible. In geography you use theory to suggest the reason, such as discharge increasing as more tributaries join the river downstream.

bullets: **Identify** anomalies on graphs by circling them and quoting the value.
**Possible human causes**: misread equipment, wrong unit, timing error, counting the same person twice.
**Possible physical causes**: a **tributary** joining, a **bridge or weir** changing the channel, a **large boulder** changing depth, a recent **storm**.
**Possible human geography causes**: a special event, road works, a bus stop or a school nearby.
If an anomaly is a **genuine feature**, keep it and explain it; if it is clearly a **mistake**, repeat the measurement or exclude it and say so.
Anomalies **affect the mean** more than the median.
Mention **repeat readings** as a way of checking whether the value is an anomaly.
core.h: Anomalies and how to deal with them
core.p: An **anomaly** (anomalous result) is a value that does not fit the overall pattern. In Figure 2 the reading at 8 km is lower than the trend. It may be a genuine feature of the place or a mistake. The enquiry must **identify** it, **suggest a reason** and decide whether to **keep** it or exclude it from calculations. Examiners like a **specific, geographical** explanation rather than just "human error".

bullets: Link your results to a **model**: the Bradshaw model for rivers, the **Burgess or Hoyt models** for urban land use (if you studied them), or **distance decay**.
Use **processes**: erosion, transport and deposition for coasts and rivers; **economic and social** reasons for urban patterns.
Use the **words from the specification**: e.g. "hydraulic action", "abrasion", "attrition", "accessibility", "land value".
Say if the result **supports** the theory or **differs**, and suggest a reason for any difference.
Use **sentence structure** such as "This is because ...", "which leads to ...", "as a result ...".
Each explanation should link a **cause** to an **effect** to the **data**.
core.p: Analysis does not stop at describing. You must **explain** why the pattern occurs by using **theory and processes**. For example, river velocity usually increases downstream because the **channel becomes more efficient**: a larger, smoother channel has less friction compared with its volume of water, so water moves faster even though the gradient decreases. In a town, pedestrian counts decrease from the CBD because the **accessibility** and **land value** are highest at the centre and shops cluster there.

bullets: Read the **enquiry question and methods** first; they give clues about the expected pattern.
**Quote data** from the resource, including units, rather than general statements.
For "calculate" questions, **show working** and use data exactly as given.
For "suggest a reason", use **geographical knowledge**, not guesses.
For "how could the presentation be improved": suggest a **better graph type**, **scale**, or additional **map** or **annotated photos**.
For "assess the usefulness": give **strengths and weaknesses**, and finish with a **judgement**.
Use **comparisons** between sites with connectives such as "whereas" and "compared with".
core.p: In Section B some questions use **data from a fieldwork enquiry you have not done**. You are given the aim, methods, and results as a table, graph or map. You use the same skills as for your own work. The question wording tells you what to do: **calculate** a statistic, **describe** a pattern, **suggest** a reason, or **assess** how useful the data are. The marks for each part are on the paper, so use them to judge how many points to write.

bullets: **Cartographic skills**: reading grid references, contour lines and map scales help in presenting fieldwork on maps.
**Graphical skills**: choosing and drawing graphs is tested across Papers 1, 2 and 3.
**Numerical skills**: mean, median and percentages appear in many topics.
**Rivers and coasts**: use of long profiles, cross sections and beach profiles to describe change.
**Urban change**: patterns of land use, quality of life and environmental quality.
**Issue evaluation**: also needs you to extract and interpret information from graphs, tables and maps.
**Conclusions and evaluation**: your analysis supplies the evidence for the next stage.
core.p: Presentation and analysis are part of every fieldwork enquiry, and they use the same skills tested in **Geographical skills** (cartographic, graphical, numerical and statistical skills). The theories needed to explain results come from your physical and human topics, so revising them helps you in this section. The next stage after analysis is the **conclusion and evaluation**.

exam: **Describe** questions: give the overall trend, quote figures with units, and mention anomalies; do not explain unless asked.
**Calculate** questions: show each step of working; marks are given for method, so write the formula and substitution.
**1-mark** questions often ask you to name a graph, read a value, or state the median/range.
**2-mark** questions: give the trend plus one figure, or the calculation with the correct unit.
**4-mark** questions: for "suggest a different way of presenting", give the method, what it would show and why it is better.
**6-mark** and **9-mark** questions: balanced evaluation of how useful the presentation or analysis was, with a judgement.
Use phrases: "shows a positive correlation", "the data are skewed by an anomaly", "median is more representative because ...".
On graphs: read from the **scale carefully**, using a ruler; state the value with the correct unit.
For map questions, refer to **the key** and quote classes, not just shades.
When completing a graph, **plot carefully**, join with a ruler if a line graph, and do not forget the **label**.
Check that your description matches the **number of marks**: 4 marks needs 4 clear points.

mistakes.r: A histogram is used for continuous grouped data, with bars touching.
mistakes.w: A bar chart can be used for continuous data like pebble size.

mistakes.r: It shows the general trend, with about equal numbers of points on either side.
mistakes.w: A line of best fit joins every point.

mistakes.r: Correlation shows a link only; use theory to suggest a cause.
mistakes.w: The data show a correlation so one variable causes the other.

mistakes.r: Use the median if there are anomalies, because the mean is distorted.
mistakes.w: The mean is always the best average.

mistakes.r: Range uses only the two extreme values; the IQR shows the spread of the middle half.
mistakes.w: The range tells you the average spread.

mistakes.r: Describe = what the data show (with figures); explain = why, using geography.
Identify them, suggest a reason and decide whether to keep or exclude them.
Marks are lost for missing titles, axis labels and units.
mistakes.w: Graph without units or a title is fine if the numbers are right.

summary: The specification expects you to present fieldwork data using suitable graphs, maps and statistics, and then analyse it by describing trends, relationships and anomalies. You must explain patterns using geographical ideas. It matters because Paper 3 Section B tests these skills on both your own and unfamiliar fieldwork.

worked.ans: (a) Mean = 79.1, median = 71. (b) Range = 117, IQR = 80. (c) Pedestrian counts decrease steadily with distance from the CBD (142 to 25 people per 5 minutes), although the 400 m site (71) is an anomaly as it is higher than at 300 m (64), possibly due to a bus stop or school nearby.
worked.q: Pedestrian counts per 5 minutes at 7 sites from the CBD outwards (0 to 600 m) were 142, 118, 96, 64, 71, 38 and 25. (a) Calculate the mean and the median. (b) Calculate the range and the IQR. (c) Describe the pattern and identify one anomaly. (6 marks)
steps: Order the data: 25, 38, 64, 71, 96, 118, 142. The middle (4th) value is 71, so the median = 71.
Lower half is 25, 38, 64 so Q1 = 38; upper half is 96, 118, 142 so Q3 = 118. IQR = 118 - 38 = 80.
Pattern: counts decrease overall with distance from the CBD, from 142 at 0 m to 25 at 600 m.
Anomaly: the 400 m site (71) is higher than the 300 m site (64), which breaks the trend.

worked.q: A traffic count rose from 80 vehicles per 10 minutes on a minor road to 128 on the main road. Calculate the percentage increase. (2 marks)

worked.ans: Velocity shows a positive correlation with distance downstream, rising from 0.20 to 0.85 m/s (0.65 m/s over 12 km, about 0.05 m/s per km). The reading at 8 km (0.30 m/s) is an anomaly, perhaps caused by a shallow rough section or large boulders increasing friction and slowing the water at that site.
worked.q: A scattergraph shows river velocity rising from 0.20 m/s at 2 km from the source to 0.85 m/s at 14 km, with one reading at 8 km of 0.30 m/s that is below the trend. Describe the relationship and suggest a reason for the anomaly. (4 marks)
steps: Overall: positive correlation, velocity increases with distance downstream.
Quote data: increase of 0.65 m/s over 12 km (about 0.05 m/s per km).
Identify the anomaly: 0.30 m/s at 8 km does not fit the trend.
Reason: a local feature such as a shallow, rough section, a large boulder or a weir slows flow; or a measurement error.
